encounters.cc: Progressive bilateral lower extremity swelling over two months

lines: Progressive bilateral lower extremity swelling over two months
The patient returns for cardiology evaluation three months after her diabetes visit.
She presents with bilateral lower extremity swelling that has progressively worsened over the past two months.
She reports that the swelling is more pronounced by the end of the day and improves slightly with elevation overnight.
She denies any chest pain, dyspnea, or recent travel.
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (10-year duration, poorly controlled)
- Osteopenia secondary to long-term corticosteroid use
Her current medications include amlodipine 10 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.

encounters.cc: Persistent, itchy, scaly rash on right nipple and areola for six months with occasional weeping

lines: Persistent, itchy, scaly rash on right nipple and areola for six months with occasional weeping

This 58-year-old female with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis on corticosteroid therapy presents with a six-month history of persistent, itchy rash on her right nipple and areola.
She reports that the rash initially appeared as a small, red, scaly patch but has since become more extensive and occasionally weeps clear fluid.
She denies any nipple discharge or palpable masses.
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (10-year duration, poorly controlled)
- Osteopenia secondary to long-term corticosteroid use
- Insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneous at bedtime
No family history of breast cancer
Smoking: Active smoker, 30 pack-years (approximately 1 pack per day).
Alcohol: Occasional (1-2 glasses of wine per month).
On physical examination, the right nipple-areolar complex is erythematous, with areas of excoriation and a small ulceration.
There is no palpable mass in either breast, and axillary lymph nodes are non-palpable.
A mammogram shows a subtle area of increased density in the right breast, without distinct masses or calcifications.
A punch biopsy of the affected skin is performed.

lines: Irregular vaginal bleeding and postcoital spotting for six months

This 59-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and prior Paget disease returns reporting that the bleeding is not associated with pain but has progressively worsened over the past two months.
She has not had a Pap smear in over 10 years.
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (10-year duration, poorly controlled)
- Osteopenia secondary to long-term corticosteroid use
Her medical history is significant for hypertension, controlled with hydrochlorothiazide.
- Insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Mother: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stroke at age 72
- Father: Coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction at age 68
- Maternal aunt: Breast cancer (invasive ductal carcinoma, age 62)
Her vital signs are within normal limits.
On physical examination, a 3 cm exophytic lesion is noted on the anterior lip of the cervix.
The lesion is friable and bleeds easily upon contact.
A pelvic exam does not reveal any vaginal or parametrial involvement.
A biopsy of the cervical lesion is performed.

encounters.cc: Recurrent episodes of severe dizziness for two weeks triggered by positional changes

lines: Recurrent episodes of severe dizziness for two weeks triggered by positional changes
The patient is a 60-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and recently diagnosed AA amyloidosis who presents with recurrent episodes of severe dizziness.
She reports that the dizziness occurs suddenly when she turns her head to the right while lying down or when she looks up to reach for items on a high shelf.
Each episode lasts for less than a minute but is severe enough to cause nausea.
She denies any hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurologic symptoms.
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (10-year duration, poorly controlled)
- Osteopenia secondary to long-term corticosteroid use
Her past medical history is significant for hypertension.
- Insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Mother: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stroke at age 72
- Father: Coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction at age 68
- Maternal aunt: Breast cancer (invasive ductal carcinoma, age 62)
Smoking: Active smoker, 30 pack-years (approximately 1 pack per day).
Alcohol: Occasional (1-2 glasses of wine per month).
On physical examination, her cardiovascular and neurologic examinations are unremarkable.
When performing the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, the patient experiences a burst of nystagmus that lasts for less than a minute and resolves spontaneously.

encounters.cc: Sudden, painless loss of vision in right eye for three hours after minor head trauma

lines: Sudden, painless loss of vision in right eye for three hours after minor head trauma

The patient is a 61-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of AA amyloidosis who presents to the emergency department for sudden, painless loss of vision in her right eye that began 3 hours ago after she accidentally struck her head on a door frame.
She reports no preceding flashes of light or floaters.
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (10-year duration, poorly controlled)
- Osteopenia secondary to long-term corticosteroid use
Her past medical history is significant for poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and long-standing hypertension.
- Insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Mother: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stroke at age 72
- Father: Coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction at age 68
- Maternal aunt: Breast cancer (invasive ductal carcinoma, age 62)
Smoking: Active smoker, 30 pack-years (approximately 1 pack per day).
Alcohol: Occasional (1-2 glasses of wine per month).
On examination, her right eye has a visual acuity of 20/250, while the left eye is 20/25.
Intraocular pressure is within normal limits, and there is no evidence of pain, redness, or photophobia.
The left eye appears normal on examination.

encounters.cc: Worsening abdominal pain, fever, and acute drop in hemoglobin requiring transfusion with subsequent respiratory distress

lines: Worsening abdominal pain, fever, and acute drop in hemoglobin requiring transfusion with subsequent respiratory distress

The patient is a 61-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis on immunosuppressive therapy, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, AA amyloidosis, and cervical squamous cell carcinoma who presented six months ago for retinal detachment.
She is admitted for evaluation of worsening abdominal pain and fever.
She is found to have complicated diverticulitis with localized perforation requiring intravenous antibiotics and supportive care.
Over the next 48 hours, her hemoglobin drops from 10.2 g/dL to 7.4 g/dL due to ongoing gastrointestinal blood loss, and she receives multiple units of packed red blood cells.
Several hours after her third transfusion, she becomes increasingly short of breath.
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (10-year duration, poorly controlled)
- Osteopenia secondary to long-term corticosteroid use
- Insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Mother: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stroke at age 72
- Father: Coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction at age 68
- Maternal aunt: Breast cancer (invasive ductal carcinoma, age 62)
Smoking: Active smoker, 30 pack-years (approximately 1 pack per day).
Alcohol: Occasional (1-2 glasses of wine per month).
Her respiratory rate is 28/min, oxygen saturation is 84% on room air, pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg.
On examination, she appears distressed and is using accessory muscles to breathe.
Lung auscultation reveals diffuse crackles bilaterally without wheezing.
Heart sounds are normal, and there is no jugular venous distension or peripheral edema.
Chest x-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with normal cardiac silhouette.
